trivia_fact: ifconfig dates back to 4.2BSD (1983) and was the standard for decades. The `ip` command (from iproute2, 1999) was written by Alexey Kuznetsov to expose Linux's more advanced networking stack (netlink). ifconfig was deprecated because it can't handle modern features like multiple IPs per interface, policy routing, or network namespaces.

The loopback address 127.0.0.1 was assigned in RFC 990 (1986). The entire 127.0.0.0/8 block (over 16 million addresses) is reserved for loopback — you can ping 127.255.255.254 and it works. This massive allocation was made when IPv4 addresses seemed unlimited. No one expected we'd run out.

The 127.0.0.0/8 range wastes over 16 million IPv4 addresses for loopback — a single address would suffice. Similarly, 0.0.0.0/8, 10.0.0.0/8, and 224-255.0.0.0 are all reserved. These early allocations are a major reason IPv4 address space ran out. IPv6 uses just ::1 for loopback.

netstat (from net-tools, 1990s) reads /proc/net/* files parsed from kernel data structures — slow on systems with thousands of connections. ss (socket statistics, from iproute2) uses netlink sockets to query the kernel directly, making it orders of magnitude faster. netstat is deprecated but stubbornly persists in tutorials.

tcpdump was named in 1988 when TCP was the primary protocol of interest. It actually captures all network traffic (UDP, ICMP, ARP, etc.) — the name is a historical artifact. The underlying library, libpcap (packet capture), has the more accurate name. Wireshark's CLI tool `tshark` also uses libpcap.

ethtool was written by David Miller (a prolific Linux networking developer) to replace the poorly standardized MII tool. It can query and change NIC settings that no other tool can: ring buffer sizes, hardware offload features, driver info, and even firmware dumps. Some features require NIC driver support.

iptables (1998) replaced ipchains, which replaced ipfwadm, which replaced the original IP firewall code. nftables (2014) replaced iptables with a cleaner architecture: a single framework for IPv4, IPv6, ARP, and bridging (iptables needed separate tools for each). Despite this, iptables remains more widely used.

Network namespaces (Linux 2.6.24, 2008) give each namespace its own network stack — interfaces, routing tables, iptables rules, even its own loopback. This is the foundation of container networking: each Docker container gets its own network namespace connected to the host via virtual ethernet (veth) pairs.

Ethernet's default MTU of 1500 bytes was chosen in the early 1980s as a compromise between throughput (bigger is better) and error recovery (smaller means less data lost per corrupted frame). The number 1500 has no mathematical significance — it was an engineering trade-off that became an unshakeable standard.

/etc/resolv.conf has used the same simple format since 4.3BSD (1986): nameserver lines with IP addresses. It supports at most 3 nameservers and has no built-in failover intelligence. Modern systems (systemd-resolved, NetworkManager) often replace it with a stub pointing to 127.0.0.53.

TCP's three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) was designed by Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn in 1974. Three messages is the theoretical minimum needed to establish reliable bidirectional communication and synchronize sequence numbers. SYN flood attacks exploit this by sending SYNs without completing the handshake.

Linux NIC bonding (combining multiple NICs into one logical interface) was inspired by Cisco's EtherChannel. The bonding driver supports 7 modes including active-backup, round-robin, and 802.3ad (LACP). Mode 4 (LACP) requires switch support, which trips up many first-time users who expect it to "just work."
